newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu to defend settlements in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu to defend settlements in U.S.

text.p: Israel's leader Benjamin Netanyahu will insist when he meets U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday that the Jewish state has a right to go on building Jewish settlements, Israel said on Thursday.
During his U.S. trip Netanyahu will also meet Jordan's King Hussein in Minnesota, where the monarch is undergoing surgery, on Sunday, Israeli spokesmen said.

"The prime minister will make clear in Washington that Israel stands by its right to build in Jerusalem and in settlements, and included in that the building will continue at Har Homa," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said.

The meeting with Clinton on Monday is part of a U.S. bid to save Middle East peace moves which were plunged into a crisis and clashes by Netanyahu's groundbreaking last month on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

"From Israel's standpoint, the purpose of the prime minister's trip to Washington is to strengthen the understanding that a basic condition of the peace process is that the Palestinian Authority keep its commitment to fight terrorism," Bazak said in a statement.
"Only after that will be made clear, will it be possible to clarify how to make progress in the peace process, including by way of the initiatives that the prime minister raised."

Israel captured Arab East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it, claiming it was part of Israel's eternal capital. Palestinians view East Jerusalem as the capital of a future independent state.
Netanyahu's office said the Israeli leader would meet King Hussein in Minnesota at the monarch's invitation.
"He will meet the king on Sunday on the way to Washington," Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan told Reuters. "The king invited him and he's going."
Israel Radio said Netanyahu could discuss with the king the fate of Mousa Mohammed Abu Marzook, a politcal leader of the militant Palestinian group Hamas who is jailed in the United States.
Israeli and U.S. officials have been trying to find ways to avoid extraditing Abu Marzook to Israel -- perhaps sending him to Jordan instead.

Israel and Jordan are partners to a 1994 peace treaty but the Jewish state's relations with the Arab world have been tense since Netanyahu started work at the Har Homa site in East Jerusalem which the Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim.
